newsitem.title: UK: Loyalists suspected of bombing Catholic.
newsitem.headline: Loyalists suspected of bombing Catholic.

text.p: A Catholic family, including a five-month-old girl, escaped unhurt on Monday in what appeared to have a bombing attack by Protestant Loyalists in breach of a two-year ceasefire.
The family was shaken but unhurt after a device exploded under their van in Larne, a busy seaport town North of Belfast. Police said it appeared to have been a purely sectarian attack.
It was the second bombing of the day after suspected IRA guerrillas fighting British rule threw two crude bombs at a police station in east Belfast. No-one was seriously hurt.
The two attacks marked a sharp escalation of violence since the start of the year and highlighted the fragility of the truce which Loyalists are supposed to be observing.

The Irish Republican Army abandoned a ceasefire in February 1996 after failing to win a seat at Belfast peace talks but their Protestant adversaries, dubbed Loyalists because they want continued links with Britain, have not announced any end to a truce they called in October 1994.
Police said the Larne attack was typical of the sort Loyalists carried out against the Catholic community, from which the IRA draws support, until their ceasefire.

Politicians close to Loyalist guerrillas are taking part in the Belfast peace talks by virtue of the truce by the gunmen but say the ceasefire is under strain because of a series of IRA attacks in Northern Ireland since last October.
They risk being expelled from the negotiations, which are chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, if their allied organisations go back to war.
The IRA launched a new campaign in Northern Ireland last October, killing one British soldier in a bombing of London's army headquarters in the province.
There have been attacks every week since, most directed against the Protestant-dominated Royal Ulster Constabulary police. No-one has been killed this year.

Police fear that the IRA is trying to goad Loyalists back to tit-for-tat reprisals to undermine the Belfast peace talks so that the winner of British elections, due by May, has to rebuild a two-year peace process.

Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the talks, say the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein can only be admitted if the IRA ends war for good. The IRA says Sinn Fein should get automatic access to the talks once there is a truce, with no other preconditions.
